## Constituencies and council areas
[edit]
The Fifth Review of the Boundary Commission for Scotland related the boundaries of new constituencies to those of Scottish local government council areas and to local government wards. Apart from a few minor adjustments, the council area boundaries dated from 1996 and the ward boundaries dated from 1999. Some council areas were grouped to form larger areas and, within these larger areas, some constituencies straddle council area boundaries.
The same council area and ward boundaries were in use when the new constituencies were first used in 2005, but ward boundaries have changed since then. New wards were introduced for the 2007 Scottish local government elections.

In December 2003, the Boundary Commission for Scotland published its final recommendations for the new Scottish constituencies boundaries. These boundaries will take effect at the next General Election.
The number of Scottish consituencies has decreased from 72 to 59. The Boundary Commission's changes have been widespread and almost all Scottish seats have been altered in some way.
This list gives an approximate tie up from old to new constituencies. Typically each new constituency contains all, or almost all, of an old constituency plus some extra parts of some other old seats. This table show the old seat which has most in common with the new seat. Where an old seat is particularly fragmented into different new constituencies it is labelled as "Disappearing".
The name of MP shown is as at the 2001 election, and that person may not be a candidate for that seat at the next election. Please consult the political parties directly to discover who their candidates will be.
The table is intended to help understand the broad outline of the new seats, but it is not exact. For precise and detailed information about each new seat, please consult the website of the Boundary Commission for Scotland.

In December 2003, the Boundary Commission for Scotland published its final recommendations for the new Scottish constituencies boundaries. These boundaries will take effect at the next General Election.
The number of Scottish consituencies has decreased from 72 to 59. The Boundary Commission's changes have been widespread and almost all Scottish seats have been altered in some way.

Typically each new constituency contains all, or almost all, of an old constituency plus some extra parts of some other old seats. This table show the old seat which has most in common with the new seat. Where an old seat is particularly fragmented into different new constituencies it is labelled as "Disappearing".
The name of MP shown is as at the 2001 election, and that person may not be a candidate for that seat at the next election. Please consult the political parties directly to discover who their candidates will be.
The table is intended to help understand the broad outline of the new seats, but it is not exact. For precise and detailed information about each new seat, please consult the website of the Boundary Commission for Scotland.

The Fifth Review of the Boundary Commission for Scotland related the boundaries of new constituencies to those of Scottish local government council areas and to local government wards. Some council areas were grouped to form larger areas and, within these larger areas, some constituencies straddle council area boundaries.

## Constituencies and council areas
[edit]
The Fifth Review of the Boundary Commission for Scotland related the boundaries of new constituencies to those of Scottish local government council areas and to local government wards. Apart from a few minor adjustments, the council area boundaries dated from 1996 and the ward boundaries dated from 1999. Some council areas were grouped to form larger areas and, within these larger areas, some constituencies straddle council area boundaries.
The same council area and ward boundaries were in use when the new constituencies were first used in 2005, but ward boundaries have changed since then. New wards were introduced for the 2007 Scottish local government elections.

Title: New Scottish Constituency Boundaries 2005
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8
In December 2003, the Boundary Commission for Scotland published its final recommendations for the new Scottish constituencies boundaries. These boundaries will take effect at the next General Election.
The number of Scottish consituencies has decreased from 72 to 59. This reduces the over-representation of Scotland at Westminster following the creation of the devolved Scottish Parliament in Edinburgh.
The Boundary Commission's changes have been widespread and almost all Scottish seats have been altered in some way.
*   Impact on 2001 results  
*   Disappearing seats  
*   Calculation details  
*   Example calculation: East Dunbartonshire  
*   Old-to-new seat converter  
*   Return to Scotland home page
I am very grateful to Raymond Baxter for the preparation and construction of these data.

## Boundaries' Impact on 2001 results
If the 2001 election had been run on the new boundaries the results would have been.
| Party | Gains | Losses | Change | Old Seats | New Seats |  
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |  
| CON | 0 | 1 | **-1** | 1 | **0** |  
| LAB | 1 | 11 | **-10** | 56 | **46** |  
| LIB | 0 | 1 | **-1** | 10 | **9** |  
| SNP | 0 | 1 | **-1** | 5 | **4** |
The one seat to "change hands" is Galloway and Upper Nithsdale held by Peter Duncan (CON). This old seat has much in common with the new seat of Dumfries and Galloway. However, Labour would have won this new seat narrowly in 2001, had the new boundaries been in force then.

## Disappearing seats
The total number of seats is decreasing by 13. Although there is no hard-and-fast definition of a "vanishing seat" the following seats are particularly broken-up and dispersed under the new boundaries.
**Old Constituency****Party****Member (as at 2001)**  
Aberdeen North LAB Malcolm Savidge  
Cunninghame South LAB Brian Donohoe  
Dumbarton LAB John McFall  
Dunfermline East LAB Gordon Brown  
Edinburgh Central LAB Alistair Darling  
Glasgow Govan LAB Mohammed Sarwar  
Glasgow Kelvin LAB George Galloway  
Hamilton North and Bellshill LAB John Reid  
Hamilton South LAB Bill Tynan  
Linlithgow LAB Tam Dalyell  
Renfrewshire West LAB James Sheridan  
Tayside North SNP Peter Wishart  
Tweeddale Ettrick and Lauderdale LIB Michael Moore
The current MPs named above may well be selected by their parties for a neighbouring new seat, but that information is not available at this time. Please contact the party concerned for details of their candidates.

## Calculation details
The following assumptions were made to calculate the 2001 implied results.
*   The Boundary Commission for Scotland's final recommendations of 11 December 2003 are assumed to be adopted unchanged.   
*   Old constituencies are assumed made up of whole new wards. This is not strictly true, but we do not think it introduces significant error.   
*   The Speaker of the House of Commons, Michael Martin, is deemed be a Labour MP. The Unionist votes in his old seat of Glasgow Springburn are assumed to represent Conservative voters.   
*   The calculation makes use of local government elections of May 2003 which show party support ward-by-ward. Where a party had no candidate in a particular ward, a subjective estimate of likely support for that party in that ward has been made. Typically a party does not stand where it would only receive small support, so this should not materially change the winning party.
The calculation is based on allocating votes in old constituencies into new ones. If the old constituency is completely contained within a new constituency, then its votes are simply transferred into the new one. If the old constituency is split between two or more new constituencies, then the calulcation is performed as follows.
Let the wards in the old constituency be called $i$, where $i = 1 , \ldots , N$. Let $j$ be the index of a particular party. Let $E \left(\right. i \left.\right)$ be the 2001 electorate in that ward. Let $E = E \left(\right. 1 \left.\right) + \ldots + E \left(\right. N \left.\right)$ be the total electorate in the old constituency.

## Calculation details
Let $G \left(\right. j \left.\right)$ be the absolute votes cast for party $j$ in the old constituency at the June 2001 General Election. Let $L \left(\right. i , j \left.\right)$ be the absolute votes cast in ward $i$ for party $j$ at the May 2003 local elections. Let $S \left(\right. j \left.\right) = L \left(\right. 1 , j \left.\right) + \ldots + L \left(\right. N , j \left.\right)$ be the total votes cast in the old constituency for party $j$ at the May 2003 local elections.
Then our formula for the implied votes in ward _i_ for party _j_ at the 2001 General Election is
$$  
V \left(\right. i , j \left.\right) = L \left(\right. i , j \left.\right) + \left(\right. G \left(\right. j \left.\right) - S \left(\right. j \left.\right) \left.\right) \frac{E \left(\right. i \left.\right)}{E} .  
$$
Or, in the less typical case where $S \left(\right. j \left.\right)$ is larger than $G \left(\right. j \left.\right)$, we use a multiplicative formula which avoids the risk of negative implied votes,
$$  
V \left(\right. i , j \left.\right) = L \left(\right. i , j \left.\right) \frac{G \left(\right. j \left.\right)}{S \left(\right. j \left.\right)} .  
$$
This formula has the desired property that $V \left(\right. 1 , j \left.\right) + \ldots + V \left(\right. N , j \left.\right) = G \left(\right. j \left.\right)$, so that the total number of party $j$ votes allocated from the old constituency equals the votes actually cast for that party.
A new constituency will then receive an additional $V \left(\right. i , j \left.\right)$ votes for party $j$ if it contains ward $i$.

In December 2003, the Boundary Commission for Scotland published its final recommendations for the new Scottish constituencies boundaries. These boundaries will take effect at the next General Election.

## Calculation details
The following assumptions were made to calculate the 2001 implied results.
*   The Boundary Commission for Scotland's final recommendations of 11 December 2003 are assumed to be adopted unchanged.   
*   Old constituencies are assumed made up of whole new wards. This is not strictly true, but we do not think it introduces significant error.   
*   The Speaker of the House of Commons, Michael Martin, is deemed be a Labour MP. The Unionist votes in his old seat of Glasgow Springburn are assumed to represent Conservative voters.   
*   The calculation makes use of local government elections of May 2003 which show party support ward-by-ward. Where a party had no candidate in a particular ward, a subjective estimate of likely support for that party in that ward has been made. Typically a party does not stand where it would only receive small support, so this should not materially change the winning party.
The calculation is based on allocating votes in old constituencies into new ones. If the old constituency is completely contained within a new constituency, then its votes are simply transferred into the new one. If the old constituency is split between two or more new constituencies, then the calulcation is performed as follows.
Let the wards in the old constituency be called $i$, where $i = 1 , \ldots , N$. Let $j$ be the index of a particular party. Let $E \left(\right. i \left.\right)$ be the 2001 electorate in that ward. Let $E = E \left(\right. 1 \left.\right) + \ldots + E \left(\right. N \left.\right)$ be the total electorate in the old constituency.
texts.4:
## Calculation details
Let $G \left(\right. j \left.\right)$ be the absolute votes cast for party $j$ in the old constituency at the June 2001 General Election. Let $L \left(\right. i , j \left.\right)$ be the absolute votes cast in ward $i$ for party $j$ at the May 2003 local elections. Let $S \left(\right. j \left.\right) = L \left(\right. 1 , j \left.\right) + \ldots + L \left(\right. N , j \left.\right)$ be the total votes cast in the old constituency for party $j$ at the May 2003 local elections.
Then our formula for the implied votes in ward _i_ for party _j_ at the 2001 General Election is
$$  
V \left(\right. i , j \left.\right) = L \left(\right. i , j \left.\right) + \left(\right. G \left(\right. j \left.\right) - S \left(\right. j \left.\right) \left.\right) \frac{E \left(\right. i \left.\right)}{E} .  
$$
Or, in the less typical case where $S \left(\right. j \left.\right)$ is larger than $G \left(\right. j \left.\right)$, we use a multiplicative formula which avoids the risk of negative implied votes,
$$  
V \left(\right. i , j \left.\right) = L \left(\right. i , j \left.\right) \frac{G \left(\right. j \left.\right)}{S \left(\right. j \left.\right)} .  
$$
This formula has the desired property that $V \left(\right. 1 , j \left.\right) + \ldots + V \left(\right. N , j \left.\right) = G \left(\right. j \left.\right)$, so that the total number of party $j$ votes allocated from the old constituency equals the votes actually cast for that party.
A new constituency will then receive an additional $V \left(\right. i , j \left.\right)$ votes for party $j$ if it contains ward $i$.
